source.title_on_document: From Planning to Revision: How AI Writing Support at Different Stages Alters Ownership

supplement.where: No separate supplement is referenced. Appendices A-I (prompts, interface, LLM prompts, survey items, quality control, grading procedure, codebook, model equations, Tables 6-8) are printed at the end of this PDF.
supplement.holds: Appendix tables in this PDF hold the arm-level adjusted means with 95% CIs (Table 6, p. 29) and the active-user robustness check (Table 8, p. 32). No standard deviations of the quality outcome by arm are printed; Figure 11c (p. 30) shows box plots only.

paper_design_summary: Prolific participants in the US, UK, and Australia wrote a 200-300 word argumentative essay in three timed stages (outline, draft, revision) and were randomly assigned to no AI, AI support for planning, an AI-generated draft from their own outline, or AI revision tools (gpt-4.1-mini). The paper measures self-reported ownership, self-reported share of ideas and text attributed to AI, and essay quality scored 0-9 on an IELTS-based rubric by an LLM grader (o4-mini) calibrated on expert grades. No creativity, novelty, or across-people diversity outcome is scored.

studies.label: Online between-subjects experiment on stage of AI writing support (argumentative essay)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Writing stage at which AI support was offered: no ai, ai plan, ai draft, ai revision. Participants were also randomly assigned to one of two sets of essay topics, then chose one of three topics.
assignment.quote: We designed our conditions to match typical AI support for writing in each stage. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions:
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 3.3; between-subjects stated p. 3, Section 3
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration mentioned. The paper calls its exclusion criteria and contrasts C1-C3 'pre-specified' (p. 5, Section 3.4; p. 7, Section 4.4) but names no registry.

arms.name: no ai
arms.description: No AI support; participant outlines, drafts, and revises alone.

arms.name: ai plan
arms.description: During planning only, participant can request AI thesis ideas (three at first, then one at a time) and full outlines for a generated thesis; drafts and revises alone.

arms.name: ai draft
arms.description: Participant writes own outline, then clicks a button for a one-shot AI-generated draft based on that outline (skips the drafting stage), then revises it.

arms.name: ai revision
arms.description: Participant plans and drafts alone; in revision can run three AI tools (argument improver, writing clarity, proof-reader) that give 2-4 suggestions each, with an option to auto-implement.

participants.exclusions: 18% of submissions were rejected before statistical analysis under pre-specified criteria (use of external AI tools, large pastes from outside the interface, outline or draft flagged >99% AI-generated with unusual interaction patterns); an additional two participants were excluded for data loss (p. 5, Section 3.4; p. 23, Appendix E). The number randomized and exclusions by arm are not given. Exclusions happened after assignment.
participants.who: Prolific workers, desktop users, English-speaking adults aged 22-65, 100% approval rate and at least 100 prior submissions; mean age 38 (SD 10); 250/253 native English speakers.
participants.country: United States, United Kingdom, or Australia (residence)
participants.quote: Our final data sample consisted of 253 participants distributed almost evenly across the four study conditions ( no ai : n=60; ai plan : n=66; ai draft : n=66; ai revision : n=61).

ai_tool.name_model: OpenAI gpt-4.1-mini, accessed August 2025 (p. 5, Section 3.3). Note: p. 6 Section 4.1 and p. 24 Appendix F.2 instead call the support model 'GPT-4o'.
ai_tool.how_used: Stage-specific tools in a side panel, not open chat: ai plan supplies thesis ideas and outlines on request (ideas_supplied); ai draft generates a full draft from the participant's outline; ai revision gives editing suggestions with auto-implementation (refinement). Use was optional in ai plan and ai revision: 43/66 (65.2%) requested at least one idea and 51/61 (83.6%) ran at least one revision tool (p. 31, Table 7). Primary analyses compare by assigned condition.

task.description: 200-300 word argumentative essay on one of three TOEFL/IELTS-style debate prompts (e.g., smartphone bans in schools, genetic editing of unborn children), written in three stages: outline, draft, revision.
task.duration: Planning max 10 min (min 60 words), drafting max 15 min (min 300 words), revision max 10 min (min 250 words); session estimated at 40 minutes. Mean time on task: no ai 25.1, ai plan 26.6, ai draft 13.7, ai revision 26.0 minutes (p. 8, Table 1).

outcomes.name: Essay quality (quality_overall), IELTS-based rubric
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Mean of three 0-9 subscores adapted from the IELTS Writing Task 2 band descriptors: quality of argument, coherence and cohesion, lexical resource and grammar. Graded by OpenAI o4-mini (reasoning effort high) prompted as an IELTS examiner with the full descriptors and 30 essays graded by an expert English-language teacher as few-shot examples; agreement with the teacher on 20 held-out essays: tolerance-based Cohen's kappa = 0.85 (pp. 6-7, Section 4.1; p. 24, Appendix F). This is a writing-quality score, not a creativity or novelty rating. The model controls for prompt fixed effects plus final word count and total time on task (both post-treatment; the paper excludes them from RQ1/RQ2 for that reason, p. 7, Section 4.2), with heteroskedasticity-robust SEs. Robustness: restricted to active tool users (p. 32, Table 8): no-ai 5.67 [5.48, 5.87], ai-plan 5.93 [5.63, 6.23] (n = 43), ai-draft 7.25 [7.03, 7.46], ai-revision 5.88 [5.60, 6.15] (n = 51).

contrasts.reported: Adjusted means (prompt-adjusted, word count and minutes at sample means), 95% CI with robust SEs: ai-draft 7.27 [7.06, 7.48] (n = 66) vs no-ai 5.69 [5.50, 5.88] (n = 60). No pairwise test of this contrast is reported.
contrasts.locator: p. 29, Table 6(c); p. 11, Section 5.4 and Figure 6a

contrasts.reported: Adjusted means, 95% CI: ai-plan 5.85 [5.62, 6.08] (n = 66) vs no-ai 5.69 [5.50, 5.88] (n = 60); text: 'quality was similar for ai plan (5.85)'. No pairwise test reported.
Adjusted means, 95% CI: ai-revision 5.79 [5.55, 6.03] (n = 61) vs no-ai 5.69 [5.50, 5.88] (n = 60); text: quality 'similar for ... ai revision (5.79)'. No pairwise test reported.

contrasts.treatment_arm: average of ai plan, ai draft, ai revision (contrast C1)
contrasts.reported: C1: '+0.62-point advantage for AI support (p < .001)' (text); Figure 6b prints C1 'No-AI vs AI avg' as -0.62 [-0.83, -0.40] (no-AI minus AI average).

contrasts.control_arm: average of ai plan and ai revision (contrast C2)
contrasts.reported: C2: ai-draft '+1.45 points higher than the average of ai-plan and ai-revision (p < .001)'; Figure 6b: 1.45 [1.14, 1.77].
C3: 'ai-plan and ai-revision statistically indistinguishable on quality'; Figure 6b: 0.06 [-0.26, 0.37].

company_involvement.description: Authors list university affiliations only (Sydney, Columbia, Johns Hopkins, Michigan). OpenAI models were used as tools; no company role in the study is stated.

eligibility.reason: People were randomly assigned to generative-AI writing support with a no-AI control (p. 4, Section 3.3), and 253 people were analyzed (p. 5, Section 3.4). But the task is an argumentative essay and the only outcome scored on the output is IELTS-style writing quality (argument, coherence, lexis/grammar) graded by an LLM (pp. 6-7, Section 4.1). No creativity, novelty, or across-people diversity outcome is scored. Ownership and idea/text attribution are self-reports. The task falls outside the codebook's creative-task scope ('essays judged for creativity'), so criterion 3 is not met unless Review 1 treats writing quality as 'usefulness'.

one_line_finding: In an online RCT with 253 Prolific writers, an AI-generated draft raised IELTS-style essay quality (adjusted mean 7.27 vs 5.69 with no AI; ai plan 5.85, ai revision 5.79; p. 29, Table 6c) and cut self-reported ownership most (4.29 vs 6.74; Table 6a), but the paper scores no creativity or diversity outcome.
open_questions: Does an IELTS-based writing-quality composite (argument quality, coherence, lexical resource and grammar) count as the 'usefulness' construct for a creativity outcome? If yes, criterion 3 could be met and the study would become core with a with_ai outcome.

The number of participants randomized is not reported; 18% of submissions were rejected after assignment for external AI use or large pastes, and exclusion rates by arm are not given. Differential exclusion by arm is possible.

The quality model adjusts for final word count and time on task, which are post-treatment variables (ai draft took 13.7 vs 25.1 minutes for no ai, p. 8, Table 1). No unadjusted arm means or SDs for quality are printed.
notes: Outcomes not listed because they are self-reports, not scored on the output: ownership ('I feel this piece of writing is truly mine', 1-7; adjusted means no-ai 6.74, ai-plan 6.30, ai-draft 4.29, ai-revision 5.57, p. 29, Table 6a), control/agency and effort items, and percent of ideas and text attributed to AI (p. 29, Table 6b). Also not listed: k-gram retention between stages (p. 8, Table 2), a within-person text-carryover measure, not a diversity or creativity measure. The paper is inconsistent on the support model (gpt-4.1-mini on p. 5 vs GPT-4o on pp. 6 and 24) and on the sign of C1 for quality (text +0.62 vs Figure 6b -0.62, which is no-AI minus AI average). Table 8 (p. 32) says 'unknown and ai draft are unchanged', apparently meaning no-ai. No data or code links are given.
